cards.text: Grab your apron, friend. Chronicles is walking through Israel's families tribe by tribe, and today we pick up the tribes still left, starting with Issachar. Issachar has four sons, and Tola's sons become heads of families, counted as mighty men of valor.

cards.question: Tola's descendants are counted in their genealogies as 22,600 mighty men of valor. When does that count happen?
On top of their five chiefs, Izrahiah's family in Issachar has 36,000 troops for battle. Why so many?

answers.text: They had many wives and children
They hired soldiers from other lands
They took many captives in battle

cards.text: Issachar's mighty men total 87,000. Then Benjamin's families roll by, then Naphtali, who gets one verse. ONE. Friend, I can't say good morning in one verse. Then Manasseh, where a man named Zelophehad has only daughters.

Next up is Ephraim, Joseph's son (Genesis 41:52). Then the list stops cold: Ezer and Elead are killed by the men of Gath, a Philistine city (1 Samuel 6:17), and the text says it happened because they went down to steal livestock.

cards.question: Ezer and Elead were Ephraim's sons. How does Ephraim take their death?

answers.text: He leaves the land for good

cards.question: Later, Ephraim's wife gives birth to another son. Ephraim names him Beriah, because ___ had come upon his house.
Sheerah, a daughter in Ephraim's family, gets a line all her own. True or false: she builds towns, including Lower and Upper Beth-horon.
Ephraim's family line runs on, son after son, all the way down to a man named Nun. Who is Nun's son?

cards.text: JOSHUA! The man who led Israel into the land after Moses (Joshua 1:1-2). Finding him in this list is like digging through a junk drawer and finding the good scissors. Joseph's descendants settle towns like Bethel, Shechem, Gezer and Megiddo.

Then comes Asher: sons, a couple of sisters, and family after family, called choice and mighty men of valor, with 26,000 fit for battle. Choice and mighty! The nicest thing anybody ever wrote on me was a price sticker that said 25 cents.

Then the list circles back to Benjamin for a closer look. Some families living in Geba are carried into exile, one man has sons in Moab, and a man named Shemed builds the towns of Ono and Lod. And watch for a name that showed up back in Ephraim's sad moment.

cards.question: In Benjamin's line, Elpaal's sons Beriah and Shema head families living in ___, and they drive out the people of ___.

cards.text: Then come the sons of Beriah, Elpaal, Shimei, Shashak and Jeroham, name after name. And yes, that's a different Beriah than Ephraim's son. This list has more Beriahs than my bakery has timers.

cards.question: All these Benjamite heads of families, the chiefs in their genealogies, live in ___.

cards.text: Then there's Jeiel, the father of Gibeon, who lives in Gibeon with his wife Maacah and a long line of sons. And then the list lands on a name every Israelite knows.

cards.question: In Benjamin's line, Ner was the father of Kish. Who was Kish's son?
Saul has four sons. True or false: one of them is Jonathan.

cards.text: Saul became Israel's king (1 Samuel 11:15), and his sons are Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab and Esh-baal. Jonathan's line runs on through Merib-baal and Micah, all the way down to Azel and his brother Eshek.

cards.question: Eshek's firstborn, Ulam, has sons who are mighty men of valor, with 150 sons and grandsons in all. What kind of fighters are Ulam's sons?

findings.problem: The last line, 'And watch for a name that showed up back in Ephraim's sad moment,' gives away the second blank on card 13. Ephraim's sad moment (card 5) named Gath. Of the five choices on card 13, Gath is the only one from that moment. Moab and Geba appear on card 12 itself, and Gibeon hasn't come up yet. The hint points straight to Gath and rules out the other choices.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later. ... A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The card says 'Saul has four sons' as a full count. 1 Chronicles 8:33 lists four sons here, but 2 Samuel 21:8 names Armoni and Mephibosheth as Saul's sons by Rizpah. The card should say that four of Saul's sons are listed, not that he has four.

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: This is a regular story card, not a summary of a long stretch: it reacts to Joshua and then lists the settlements. It has four sentences: 'JOSHUA!', the line saying who he is, the junk drawer joke, and the towns.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The joke 'This list has more Beriahs than my bakery has timers' doesn't click. So far the baker has seen only two Beriahs named: Ephraim's son on card 7 and Elpaal's son on card 13. A bakery with six stations would have plenty of timers, so the comparison either says he owns one timer or makes a huge number out of two names. A stranger would say 'huh?'

rule.text: It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining. If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The storyteller line 'And then the list lands on a name every Israelite knows' states a fact the text doesn't give, namely that every Israelite knew Saul's name. It should carry the moment without making a claim, like 'And then the list lands on a name you'll know.'

rule.text: Papa Dorin can add a storyteller's line to carry the moment, like "But the Lord isn't finished with him," as long as it adds no facts.

findings.problem: The whole passage, 1 Chronicles 7:1-8:40, is a genealogy with census counts and town lists, and it contains a few short stories: Ephraim's loss, Sheerah's towns, Beriah and Shema driving out Gath. The long-stretch rule says to sum up a stretch in one story card, says a stretch never gets a choice card or a stop of its own, and says a short story inside a stretch gets no choice cards. Followed literally, this passage could not have a stop at all, and it could not meet the rule that choice cards are equal to or more than story cards. The walkthrough instead uses several summary cards (cards 4, 11, 12 and 14) and 11 choice cards on genealogy details (cards 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 13, 15, 17, 18 and 20).
findings.question: When a passage is entirely a long stretch, like a genealogy chapter, how should Prep be built? May it break the stretch into several summary cards and ask choice cards about the standout details and short stories inside it, or should it be handled some other way?

findings.problem: The summary story cards run past 2 sentences: card 4 has five, and cards 11, 12 and 14 have three each. 'What bite-sized means' says every story card after the opening is 1 to 2 sentences. But the genealogy example in 'Long stretches that don't move the passage' is a single good story card with four sentences, and 'a summary story card for a long stretch' is described as one beat.
findings.question: Can a summary story card for a long stretch go past 2 sentences, as the Genesis 5 example does? If so, what is the limit?
